title: Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth; no science data since Nov 14
verification: NASA JPL release of Nov 19, 2026: Voyager 1 reached one light-day (about 16.1 billion miles, 25.9 billion km) at 2:16 a.m. PST Nov 18; signal confirmed 24 hours later; no science or engineering data since Nov 14, carrier signal still received; power drops about 4 watts a year, three devices swapped for lower-power ones; instruments expected to run until at least 50th launch anniversary next summer; entered interstellar space in 2012; about 38,000 mph; daily listening, weekly commands. Two-day command round trip follows from the 24-hour one-way light time (qz.com also says fixes take 2 days). Single primary source (NASA), cited as such.

slides.headline: Ask Voyager 1 a question. Wait 48 hours.

image.credit: Artist's concept of Voyager. NASA/JPL / Wikimedia Commons, Public domain

slides.text:
On November 18, Voyager 1 passed one light-day from Earth.
That is about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion km).
A radio signal now needs 24 hours to get there.

image.credit: Photo: NASA on The Commons / Wikimedia Commons, Public domain

slides.text:
NASA confirmed the milestone a day later, when the probe's signal finally reached Earth.
Engineers listen every day and send commands once a week.
Every command and its reply takes two days.

image.credit: Photo: NASA / Wikimedia Commons, Public domain

slides.text:
There is a catch.
Since November 14, NASA has received no science or engineering data from Voyager 1.
It still sends a bare carrier signal, enough to prove it is there. Engineers are working on why.

image.credit: Photo: Artist's concept. NASA/Walt Feimer / Wikimedia Commons, Public domain

slides.text:
Its nuclear power source loses about 4 watts a year.
To stretch it, engineers switched off three devices and turned on lower-power substitutes.
NASA says that move carried some risk.

Someday Voyager 1 will stop answering.
We will learn about it a day later.

image.credit: Photo: NASA/JPL-Caltech / Wikimedia Commons, Public domain

caption:
Voyager 1 just crossed a line no spacecraft has crossed before: it is now one light-day from Earth.

NASA says the probe reached that distance at 2:16 a.m. Pacific time on November 18, 2026. One light-day is about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion km). Radio waves travel at the speed of light, so a message sent to Voyager 1 now takes a full 24 hours to arrive, and the answer takes another 24 to come back.

The team heard from the probe a day after the milestone. It is traveling about 38,000 miles per hour in interstellar space, which it entered in 2012. Engineers listen to it every day and send commands once a week.

But NASA has had no science or engineering data from Voyager 1 since November 14. The spacecraft is still sending a carrier signal, and that is how the team confirmed the milestone. They are now analyzing the data problem.

Power is the long-term worry. The plutonium-powered generator loses about 4 watts a year. Engineers switched off three devices and moved to three lower-power ones, a move NASA says carried some risk. The goal is to keep the current science instruments running until at least the 50th launch anniversaries of both Voyagers next summer.

Source: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory
